headline: High: shared write-capable, networked agents can conflict and cascade errors; prompt-injection and leakage are plausible via shared files/MCP.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, and agent_b has a writable scratchpad plus autonomous execution, so content from one can plausibly be fed into the other as instructions. No direct shared-channel documentation exists, so uncertainty pushes this above low. The pairwise pathway is inferred from both profiles.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests agent_a stdout or scratchpad content as instructions, injection is possible.
IF a shared MCP or file bridge is configured between the agents, attacker-controlled text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction parsing from agent outputs.
Separate scratchpads and working directories.
Require provenance tags on inter-agent messages.
Add a human review step before forwarding outputs.
requires-engineering: enforce schema validation for all cross-agent payloads.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures, while agent_b touches financial and market data and writes to .dexter/scratchpad/. If they share a workspace or files are forwarded, sensitive material can leak across the pair. The profiles document file and network surfaces, but not isolation, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory tree, file contents can cross-contaminate.
IF agent_b uploads scratchpad contents to external APIs, any leaked agent_a material can leave the environment.
mitigations: Use separate per-agent workspaces.
Restrict shared files to redacted summaries.
Rotate any exposed API keys or signatures.
Audit outbound requests for sensitive fields.
requires-engineering: add DLP filters on file and API egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and use MCP; agent_b has broad network egress and autonomous execution. Both support multiple instances, so concurrent writes and external actions can collide on shared mutable resources. Because no locking or isolation is documented, the conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository or filesystem path, write conflicts can occur.
IF both agents run concurrently without locks, one agent can overwrite the other's state.
mitigations: Assign disjoint repositories or directories.
Serialize write operations with a lock file.
Disable concurrent runs on shared state.
Review git diffs before merge.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can emit MCP/stdout-driven outputs and agent_b runs autonomously with access to external APIs, so B may treat A's output as actionable input. If A produces incorrect facts or malformed instructions, B can propagate them into downstream actions or reports. No verification step is documented, so the cascade can be irreversible.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without verification, errors can cascade.
IF agent_b uses A-generated facts in API calls or reports, downstream harm can persist.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B acts on A's output.
Require citations or source links for factual claims.
Limit B to read-only evaluation of A outputs.
Log and diff all handoffs between agents.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating before external actions.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts, repository metadata, and signatures, while agent_b handles financial and market data and sends requests to multiple external APIs. The profiles do not document residency, retention, or DPA alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined data handling and egress patterns.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is processed alongside agent_a prompts or metadata, retention obligations may diverge.
IF external APIs retain agent_b inputs longer than the operator's policy, compliance gaps emerge.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent.
Block regulated data from external APIs unless approved.
Document retention and deletion settings for each API.
Keep audit logs of cross-border transfers.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing.
